newsitem.title: GERMANY: Mercedes CEO expects 1996 sales at 75 bln marks.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes CEO expects 1996 sales at 75 bln marks.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz chief executive officer Helmut Werner said on Thursday that he still expected the German car and truck maker to report 1996 sales of about 75 billion marks ($49.7 billion).
Werner told a news briefing at the IAA truck exhibition that volumes for the first eight months of the year at Mercedes, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, rose nine percent to 50.9 billion marks.
He also said he expected "record sales" in the company's commercial vehicle side and for sales to top the 320,000 units sold in 1995.

"Expanding our commercial vehicle business unit will be one of the main focal points for the further development of our company," Werner said in the text of a speech for a company news conference at the exhibition. ($ = 1.51 German Marks)
Werner said Mercedes "has developed according to plan in every respect" so far during 1996 for both car sales as well as in the commercial vehicle sector.
Sales of Mercedes cars were up 10 percent so far this year and would grow to well over 600,000 units for 1996, he said.
Sales volumes in Mercedes' commercial vehicle sector during the first eight months of 1996 were up six percent over year-ago levels, reaching 221,000 vehicles worldwide, he said.
"In view of our success on the passenger car side, some people may overlook the fact that we have sold more commercial vehicles this year than ever before in our history," he said.
Werner also described the business trend in the bus, coach and van sectors as "exceptionally positive".
Mercedes was "enjoying varied degrees of success in Europe and overseas," he said, noting the market trends were running counter to one another in Germany and the rest of Europe.
While orders in the German commercial vehicle market were beginning to pick up again throughout the industry, business in the rest of Europe was starting to flag, Werner said.
Werner also said the reorganisation of Mercedes' European bus activities under the marque names Setra and Mercedes-Benz was showing benefits.
He said sales of over 3,500 buses weighing more than eight tonnes during the first eight months of 1996 exceeded year-ago sales by about 28 percent.
"Having made losses in the European bus market for many years, our Evobus operations are now showing results," he said.

In the van sector, Werner said Mercedes was "enjoying particular success" both in terms of sales figures and incoming orders. Mercedes sold 76,500 units, increasing its van sales in the west European market by 26 percent.

Mercedes, which was to unveil its new Vito and Sprinter vans at the exhibition, said it now had a European market share in the van class of 14 percent, about 2.2 percentage points higher than year-ago levels.
At its U.S. truck subsidiary Freightliner, Werner said sales were up 10 percent despite what he called "a crumbling U.S. market".
In Latin America, Werner said the Mercedes commercial vehicle units in Argentina and Brazil had made a comeback against the backdrop of what he believed was sustained economic development.
But he said "the worst is yet to come" in Brazil. The market was in "exceptionally poor state of health" and sales at Mercedes-Benz do Brazil were down about one-third from year-ago levels.
Werner said Mercedes was keenly interested in the Chinese market, noting the recent announcement of a coach-building joint venture in the Chinese province of Yangzhou.
He also said Freightliner would start production in mid-1997 in China of special trucks weighing more than 14 tonnes, with annual production to reach up to 4,000 units.
--John Gilardi, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
